title: Choosing statistical representations
summary: Choose a statistical display by matching its purpose, data type, audience and required detail.
objectives: Compare the strengths and limits of dot diagrams, histograms, stem-and-leaf diagrams and tables.
Select a representation for discrete or continuous data.
Justify a choice using the information it preserves or hides.

blocks.text: A useful representation answers the intended question. Dot diagrams (also called dot plots) show every observation as a dot, so repeats and gaps are visible in a small set of whole-number values within a narrow range. Stem-and-leaf diagrams keep the exact value of every observation in order, which suits a small set of values spread over several tens. Histograms show the shape of a large set of grouped continuous measurements, but individual values are lost. Frequency tables give compact counts for each value or class and support calculation.

A quick way to choose between a dot diagram and a stem-and-leaf diagram: if the values are a few whole numbers close together, such as shoe sizes 36 to 42, use a dot diagram; if they spread over several tens, such as the test marks from 52 to 96 in the diagram, use a stem-and-leaf diagram, because a dot diagram would need a number line with 45 places for only 15 dots.

sections.title: Account for scale and sample size

blocks.text: A display that works for 20 observations may fail for 2,000. Dot plots and stem-and-leaf diagrams can become crowded, while grouping makes a histogram scalable but sacrifices exact individual values. Choose class widths deliberately because wide classes can hide local structure.

A strong justification names both a benefit and a cost. For example, a histogram clearly compares distribution shape across many measurements, but exact readings cannot be recovered. Avoid selecting a chart only because it looks familiar.

sections.title: Worked example: choose for exact retrieval

prompt.text: Fifteen test marks between 52 and 96 must stay individually recoverable while showing their distribution. Choose a representation.

content.text: The data set is small and numerical, so every value can be shown.
The marks spread over five tens, so a dot diagram would need a scale from 52 to 96 with many empty places.
A stem-and-leaf diagram with stems 5 to 9, as in the diagram, keeps every exact mark in order and shows the shape.

sections.verification_note: Every leaf can be decoded with the key, so no mark is lost: the diagram holds 3 + 5 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 15 leaves, one for each mark.

sections.title: Worked example: choose for a large continuous sample

prompt.text: Two thousand reaction times must be compared by the shape of their distribution, not by looking up individual values. Choose a representation.

content.text: The data are continuous and very numerous.
Use a histogram, with frequency density if the class widths differ.

sections.verification_note: A dot diagram or stem-and-leaf diagram with 2 000 entries would be unreadable; a histogram with about ten classes shows the shape clearly.

prompt.text: Use code 1 for dot diagram and 2 for histogram. Which code suits 500 grouped continuous measurements?

feedback.text: A histogram communicates the shape of a large grouped continuous dataset.

blocks.text: Dot diagram: a few close whole-number values. Stem-and-leaf diagram: a small set of exact values over several tens. Histogram: many grouped continuous measurements. Frequency table: compact counts for calculation.
